findings.trigger: A channel's 'control' permission is revoked after its Admin Overview panel was posted while it still had that permission. The panel is a persistent view (View(timeout=None), custom_id keyed only by channel_id, so it never expires). A user who is still on the global admin list (admins.json) opens that now-unauthorized channel and presses 'Restart All' or 'Stop All': AdminOverviewRestartAllButton.callback (line 190-191) and AdminOverviewStopAllButton.callback (line 264-265) check only admin_service.is_user_admin_async(user_id); the confirm buttons ConfirmRestartAllButton.callback / ConfirmStopAllButton.callback (which do the actual docker_action_service_first calls) check no permission at all. None of the four ever calls _channel_has_permission(channel_id, 'control') (cogs/control_helpers.py:96) for self.channel_id, so every active container in the whole instance is restarted/stopped even though the channel itself no longer grants control.
findings.suggestion: Re-check the CURRENT channel permission for self.channel_id (the way control_ui.py:304 was fixed to read only the live permission) in addition to, or as the actual gate instead of, the global admin check, so an old panel in a demoted channel loses its effect immediately as decided for Z5.
findings.unsure_why: This file alone does not show whether the code that posts/refreshes the Admin Overview message (out of this section) deletes or rebuilds the view without these buttons once a channel's control permission is revoked, which would close the window described here. I also cannot rule out that this is meant to be a documented admin override for control channels (comparable to B12 for the scheduler) that was simply never written down in SPEC.md the way B12 was - B2's own stated scope is status channels only, not control channels, which is why I lean toward this being a gap rather than an intended exception.

findings.trigger: Inside ConfirmRestartAllButton.callback's per-container loop, the only exceptions caught around docker_action_service_first are asyncio.TimeoutError and (RuntimeError, OSError) (line 542-546). If that call raises any other exception type partway through the loop (e.g. a docker-library error), it escapes the loop; the surrounding except at line 570 only catches (ImportError, KeyError, RuntimeError, asyncio.TimeoutError), which does not match either, so no followup.send ever runs. finally still releases _bulk_operation_in_progress, but the admin gets no message at all about how many containers were already restarted before the crash. The identical pattern exists in ConfirmStopAllButton.callback (inner catch line 719-723, outer catch line 747).
findings.suggestion: Give the outer except (or a final bare except) in both confirm-button callbacks a fallback branch that still reports whatever counts were reached, instead of leaving the admin with no result summary when an unlisted exception type surfaces.
findings.unsure_why: docker_action_service_first's implementation is outside this section, so I cannot say which exception types it can realistically raise beyond RuntimeError/OSError; this is only a gap in the code's own exception-type coverage, not a confirmed reachable failure. Both names this affects (cogs/admin_overview.py:433 and :610) are already recorded as 'finding' against F1 in the verdicts list, so this second issue at the same two functions has no verdict entry of its own.

findings.trigger: If load_tasks() (services/scheduling/scheduler.py, out of this section) raises anything other than RuntimeError - e.g. an OSError or a JSON-parsing error while reading the tasks file - schedule_task_id_select has no matching handler: the inner per-task catch (line 401) and the outer catch (line 406-408) both name only RuntimeError. The exception then propagates out of the autocomplete callback instead of the function returning [], so the '/schedule_delete' task-ID dropdown shows no options with none of the intended 'Error in schedule_task_id_select' log line to explain why.
findings.suggestion: Broaden both except clauses to cover the I/O/parsing errors load_tasks() can raise, the way schedule_container_select already catches a wider set of exception types for its own data source.
findings.unsure_why: load_tasks()'s implementation is outside this section, so I cannot confirm which exception types it can actually raise; if it never raises anything but RuntimeError in practice, this is not reachable.

notes: cogs/autocomplete_handlers.py:42 schedule_container_select builds active_docker_data_set from a live Docker/API status query (lines 64-90) but never reads that set again - the choices returned always come from the configured servers list, not from it. No behaviour difference results (the comment at line 93-97 says listing configured, schedulable containers is the actual goal), so this is dead computation rather than a graded finding, but it does mean the Docker-status fallback path (line 83-90) is also unreachable in terms of output. cogs/control_helpers.py:172 validate_custom_address's own docstring warns that this exact kind of duplicated security check caused a real Z5 break elsewhere (the task-delete button existed twice, one copy missing the channel check) and says this check 'stood twice ... in control_ui.py and status_info_integration.py'; both of those files are outside this section, so I could not verify whether they now actually call this shared function or still carry their own local copies that could drift from it again. Separately, validate_custom_address's hostname branch accepts a port of up to 5 digits without checking it is <= 65535 (e.g. 'host:99999' validates as True); I have no visibility into what a downstream consumer does with an out-of-range port, so I could not state a concrete trigger and did not turn this into a finding.
